l: Out in the fields this autumn day
They’re busy reaping grain;
I sought for shelter ’neath this roof,
But fear I sought in vain,—
My sleeve is wet with rain.
hyakunin-1.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あきのたの かりほのいほの とまをあらみ わがころもでは つゆにぬれつつ

l: The spring has gone, the summer’s come,
And I can just descry
The peak of Ama-no-kagu,
Where angels of the sky
Spread their white robes to dry.
hyakunin-2.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: はるすぎて なつきにけらし しろたへの ころもほすてふ あまのかぐやま

l: Long is the mountain pheasant’s tail
That curves down in its flight;
But longer still, it seems to me,
Left in my lonely plight,
Is this unending night.
hyakunin-3.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あしびきの やまどりのをの しだりをの ながながしよを ひとりかもねむ

l: I started off along the shore,
The sea shore at Tago,
And saw the white and glist’ning peak
Of Fuji all aglow
Through falling flakes of snow.
hyakunin-4.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: たごのうらに うちいでてみれば しろたへの ふじのたかねに ゆきはふりつつ

l: I hear the stag’s pathetic call
Far up the mountain side,
While tramping o’er the maple leaves
Wind-scattered far and wide
This sad, sad autumn tide.
hyakunin-5.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: おくやまに もみぢふみわけ なくしかの こゑきくときぞ あきはかなしき

l: When on the Magpies’ Bridge I see
The Hoar-frost King has cast
His sparkling mantle, well I know
The night is nearly past,
Daylight approaches fast.
hyakunin-6.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: かさゝぎの わたせるはしに おくしもの しろきをみれば よぞふけにける

l: While gazing up into the sky,
My thoughts have wandered far;
Methinks I see the rising moon
Above Mount Mikasa
At far-off Kasuga.
hyakunin-7.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あまのはら ふりさけみれば かすがなる みかさのやまに いでしつきかも

l: My home is near the Capital,
My humble cottage bare
Lies south-east on Mount Uji; so
The people all declare
My life’s a ‘Hill of Care’.
hyakunin-8.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: わがいほは みやこのたつみ しかぞすむ よをうぢやまと ひとはいふなり

l: The blossom’s tint is washed away
By heavy showers of rain;
My charms, which once I prized so much,
Are also on the wane,—
Both bloomed, alas! in vain.
hyakunin-9.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: はなのいろは うつりにけりな いたづらに わがみよにふる ながめせしまに

l: The stranger who has travelled far,
The friend with welcome smile,
All sorts of men who come and go
Meet at this mountain stile,—
They meet and rest awhile.
hyakunin-10.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: これやこの ゆくもかへるも わかれては しるもしらぬも あふさかのせき

l: Oh! Fishers in your little boats,
Quick! tell my men, I pray,
They’ll find me at Yasoshima,
I’m being rowed away
Far off across the bay.
hyakunin-11.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: わたのはら やそしまかけて こぎいでぬと ひとにはつげよ あまのつりぶね

l: Oh stormy winds, bring up the clouds,
And paint the heavens grey;
Lest these fair maids of form divine
Should angel wings display,
And fly far far away.
hyakunin-12.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あまつかぜ くものかよひぢ ふきとぢよ をとめのすがた しばしとどめむ

l: The Mina stream comes tumbling down
From Mount Tsukuba’s height;
Strong as my love, it leaps into
A pool as black as night
With overwhelming might.
hyakunin-13.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: つくばねの みねよりおつる みなのがは こひぞつもりて ふちとなりぬる

l: Ah! why does love distract my thoughts,
Disordering my will!
I’m like the pattern on the cloth
Of Michinoku hill,—
All in confusion still.
hyakunin-14.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: みちのくの しのぶもぢずり たれゆゑに みだれそめにし われならなくに

l: Mother, for thy sake I have been
Where the wakana grow,
To bring thee back some fresh green leaves;
And see—my koromo
Is sprinkled with the snow!
hyakunin-15.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: きみがため はるののにいでて わかなつむ わがころもでに ゆきはふりつつ

l: If breezes on Inaba’s peak
Sigh through the old pine tree,
To whisper in my lonely ears
That thou dost pine for me,—
Swiftly I’ll fly to thee.
hyakunin-16.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: たちわかれ いなばのやまの みねにおふる まつとしきかば いまかへりこむ

l: All red with leaves Tatsuta’s stream
So softly purls along,
The everlasting Gods themselves,
Who judge ’twixt right and wrong,
Ne’er heard so sweet a song.
hyakunin-17.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ちはやぶる かみよもきかず たつたがは からくれなゐに みづくくるとは

l: To-night on Sumi-no-ye beach
The waves alone draw near;
And, as we wander by the cliffs,
No prying eyes shall peer,
No one shall dream we’re here.
hyakunin-18.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: すみのえの きしによるなみ よるさへや ゆめのかよひぢ ひとめよくらむ

l: Short as the joints of bamboo reeds
That grow beside the sea
On pebble beach at Naniwa,
I hope the time may be,
When thou ’rt away from me.
hyakunin-19.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: なにはがた みじかきあしの ふしのまも あはでこのよを すぐしてよとや

l: We met but for a moment, and
I’m wretched as before;
The tide shall measure out my life,
Unless I see once more
The maid, whom I adore.
hyakunin-20.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: わびぬれば いまはたおなじ なにはなる みをつくしても あはむとぞおもふ

l: The moon that shone the whole night through
This autumn morn I see,
As here I wait thy well-known step,
For thou didst promise me—
‘I’ll surely come to thee.’
hyakunin-21.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: いまこむと いひしばかりに ながつきの ありあけのつきを まちいでつるかな

l: The mountain wind in autumn time
Is well called ‘hurricane’;
It hurries canes and twigs along,
And whirls them o’er the plain
To scatter them again.
hyakunin-22.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ふくからに あきのくさきの しをるれば むべやまかぜを あらしといふらむ

l: This night the cheerless autumn moon
Doth all my mind enthrall;
But others also have their griefs,
For autumn on us all
Hath cast her gloomy pall.
hyakunin-23.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: つきみれば ちゞにものこそ かなしけれ わがみひとつの あきにはあらねど

l: I bring no prayers on coloured silk
To deck thy shrine to-day,
But take instead these maple leaves,
That grow at Tamuké;
Finer than silk are they.
hyakunin-24.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: このたびは ぬさもとりあへず たむけやま もみぢのにしき かみのまにまに

l: I hear thou art as modest as
The little creeping spray
Upon Mount Ōsaka, which hides
Beneath the grass; then, pray,
Wander with me to-day.
hyakunin-25.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: なにしおはば あふさかやまの さねかづら ひとにしられで くるよしもがな

l: The maples of Mount Ogura,
If they could understand,
Would keep their brilliant leaves, until
The Ruler of this land
Pass with his royal band.
hyakunin-26.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: をぐらやま みねのもみぢば こゝろあらば いまひとたびの みゆきまたなむ

l: Oh! rippling River Izumi,
That flows through Mika plain,
Why should the maid I saw but now
And soon shall see again
Torment my love-sick brain?
hyakunin-27.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: みかのはら わきてながるる いづみがは いつみきとてか こひしかるらむ

l: The mountain village solitude
In winter time I dread;
It seems as if, when friends are gone,
And trees their leaves have shed,
All men and plants are dead.
hyakunin-28.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: やまざとは ふゆぞさびしさ まさりける ひとめもくさも かれぬとおもへば

l: It was a white chrysanthemum
I came to take away;
But, which are coloured, which are white,
I’m half afraid to say,
So thick the frost to-day!
hyakunin-29.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: こゝろあてに をらばやをらむ はつしもの おきまどはせる しらぎくのはな

l: I hate the cold unfriendly moon,
That shines at early morn;
And nothing seems so sad and grey,
When I am left forlorn,
As day’s returning dawn.
hyakunin-30.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ありあけの つれなくみえし わかれより あかつきばかり うきものはなし

l: Surely the morning moon, I thought,
Has bathed the hill in light;
But, no; I see it is the snow
That, falling in the night,
Has made Yoshino white.
hyakunin-31.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あさぼらけ ありあけのつきと みるまでに よしののさとに ふれるしらゆき

l: The stormy winds of yesterday
The maple branches shook;
And see! a mass of crimson leaves
Has lodged within that nook,
And choked the mountain brook.
hyakunin-32.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: やまがはに かぜのかけたる しがらみは ながれもあへぬ もみぢなりけり

l: The spring has come, and once again
The sun shines in the sky;
So gently smile the heavens, that
It almost makes me cry,
When blossoms droop and die.
hyakunin-33.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ひさかたの ひかりのどけき はるのひに しづごころなく はなのちるらむ

l: Gone are my old familiar friends,
The men I used to know;
Yet still on Takasago beach
The same old pine trees grow,
That I knew long ago.
hyakunin-34.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: たれをかも しるひとにせむ たかさごの まつもむかしの ともならなくに

l: The village of my youth is gone,
New faces meet my gaze;
But still the blossoms at thy gate,
Whose perfume scents the ways,
Recall my childhood’s days.
hyakunin-35.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ひとはいさ こゝろもしらず ふるさとは はなぞむかしの かににほひける

l: Too short the lovely summer night,
Too soon ’tis passed away;
I watched to see behind which cloud
The moon would chance to stay,
And here’s the dawn of day!
hyakunin-36.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: なつのよは まだよひながら あけぬるを くものいづこに つきやどるらむ

l: This lovely morn the dewdrops flash
Like diamonds on the grass—
A blaze of sparkling jewels! But
The autumn wind, alas!
Scatters them as I pass.
hyakunin-37.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: しらつゆに かぜのふきしく あきののは つらぬきとめぬ たまぞちりける

l: My broken heart I don’t lament,
To destiny I bow;
But thou hast broken solemn oaths,—
I pray the Gods may now
Absolve thee from thy vow.
hyakunin-38.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: わすらるる みをばおもはず ちかひてし ひとのいのちの をしくもあるかな

l: ’Tis easier to hide the reeds
Upon the moor that grow,
Than try to hide the ardent love
That sets my cheeks aglow
For somebody I know.
hyakunin-39.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あさぢふの をののしのはら しのぶれど あまりてなどか ひとのこひしき

l: Alas! the blush upon my cheek,
Conceal it as I may,
Proclaims to all that I’m in love,
Till people smile and say—
‘Where are thy thoughts to-day?’
hyakunin-40.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: しのぶれど いろにいでにけり わがこひは ものやおもふと ひとのとふまで

l: Our courtship, that we tried to hide,
Misleading is to none;
And yet how could the neighbours guess,
That I had yet begun
To fancy any one?
hyakunin-41.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: こひすてふ わがなはまだき たちにけり ひとしれずこそ おもひそめしか

l: Our sleeves, all wet with tears, attest
That you and I agree
That to each other we’ll be true,
Till Pine-tree Hill shall be
Sunk far beneath the sea.
hyakunin-42.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ちぎりきな かたみにそでを しぼりつつ すゑのまつやま なみこさじとは

l: How desolate my former life,
Those dismal years, ere yet
I chanced to see thee face to face;
’Twere better to forget
Those days before we met.
hyakunin-43.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あひみての のちのこころに くらぶれば むかしはものを おもはざりけり

l: To fall in love with womankind
Is my unlucky fate;
If only it were otherwise,
I might appreciate
Some men, whom now I hate.
hyakunin-44.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あふことの たえてしなくば なかなかに ひとをもみをも うらみざらまし
ro: Hito wo mo mi wo mo

l: I dare not hope my lady-love
Will smile on me again;
She knows no pity, and my life
I care not to retain,
Since all my prayers are vain.
hyakunin-45.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あはれとも いふべきひとは おもほえで みのいたづらに なりぬべきかな

l: The fishing-boats are tossed about,
When stormy winds blow strong;
With rudder lost, how can they reach
The port for which they long?
So runs the old love-song.
hyakunin-46.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ゆらのとを わたるふなびと かぢをたえ ゆくへもしらぬ こひのみちかな

l: My little temple stands alone,
No other hut is near;
No one will pass to stop and praise
Its vine-grown roof, I fear,
Now that the autumn ’s here.
hyakunin-47.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: やへむぐら しげれるやどの さびしきに ひとこそみえね あきはきにけり

l: The waves that dash against the rocks
Are broken by the wind
And turned to spray; my loving heart
Is broken too, I find,
Since thou art so unkind.
hyakunin-48.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: かぜをいたみ いはうつなみの おのれのみ くだけてものを おもふころかな

l: My constancy to her I love
I never will forsake;
As surely as the Palace Guards
Each night their watch-fire make
And guard it till daybreak.
hyakunin-49.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: みかきもり ゑじのたくひの よるはもえ ひるはきえつつ ものをこそおもへ

l: Death had no terrors, Life no joys,
Before I met with thee;
But now I fear, however long
My life may chance to be,
’Twill be too short for me!
hyakunin-50.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: きみがため をしからざりし いのちさへ ながくもがなと おもひけるかな

l: Though love, like blisters made from leaves
Grown on Mount Ibuki,
Torments me more than I can say,
My lady shall not see,
How she is paining me.
hyakunin-51.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: かくとだに えやはいぶきの さしもぐさ さしもしらじな もゆるおもひを

l: Although I know the gentle night
Will surely follow morn,
Yet, when I’m wakened by the sun,
Turn over, stretch and yawn—
How I detest the dawn!
hyakunin-52.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あけぬれば くるるものとは しりながら なほうらめしき あさぼらけかな

l: All through the long and dreary night
I lie awake and moan;
How desolate my chamber feels,
How weary I have grown
Of being left alone!
hyakunin-53.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: なげきつつ ひとりぬるよの あくるまは いかにひさしき ものとかはしる

l: How difficult it is for men
Not to forget the past!
I fear my husband’s love for me
Is disappearing fast;
This day must be my last.
hyakunin-54.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: わすれじの ゆくすゑまでは かたければ けふをかぎりの いのちともがな

l: This waterfall’s melodious voice
Was famed both far and near;
Although it long has ceased to flow,
Yet still with memory’s ear
Its gentle splash I hear.
hyakunin-55.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: たきのおとは たえてひさしく なりぬれど なこそながれて なほきこえけれ

l: My life is drawing to a close,
I cannot longer stay,
A pleasant memory of thee
I fain would take away;
So visit me, I pray.
hyakunin-56.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あらざらむ このよのほかの おもひでに いまひとたびの あふこともがな

l: I wandered forth this moonlight night,
And some one hurried by;
But who it was I could not see,—
Clouds driving o’er the sky
Obscured the moon on high.
hyakunin-57.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: めぐりあひて みしやそれとも わかぬまに くもがくれにし よはのつきかな

l: As fickle as the mountain gusts
That on the moor I’ve met,
’Twere best to think no more of thee,
And let thee go. But yet
I never can forget.
hyakunin-58.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ありまやま ゐなのささはら かぜふけば いでそよひとを わすれやはする

l: Waiting and hoping for thy step,
Sleepless in bed I lie,
All through the night, until the moon,
Leaving her post on high,
Slips sideways down the sky.
hyakunin-59.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: やすらはで ねなましものを さよふけて かたぶくまでの つきをみしかな

l: So long and dreary is the road,
That I have never been
To Ama-no-Hashidate;
Pray, how could I have seen
The verses that you mean?
hyakunin-60.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: おほえやま いくののみちの とほければ まだふみもみず あまのはしだて

l: The double cherry trees, which grew
At Nara in past days,
Now beautify this Palace, and
Their blossoms all ablaze
Perfume the royal ways.
hyakunin-61.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: いにしへの ならのみやこの やへざくら けふここのへに にほひぬるかな

l: Too long to-night you’ve lingered here,
And, though you imitate
The crowing of a cock, ’twill not
Unlock the tollbar gate;
Till daylight must you wait.
hyakunin-62.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: よをこめて とりのそらねは はかるとも よにあふさかの せきはゆるさじ

l: If we could meet in privacy,
Where no one else could see,
Softly I’d whisper in thy ear
This little word from me—
‘I’m dying, Love, for thee.’
hyakunin-63.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: いまはただ おもひたえなむ とばかりを ひとづてならで いふよしもがな

l: So thickly lies the morning mist,
That I can scarcely see
The fish-nets on the river bank,
The River of Uji,
Past daybreak though it be.
hyakunin-64.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あさぼらけ うぢのかはぎり たえだえに あらはれわたる せぜのあじろぎ

l: Be not displeased, but pardon me,
If still my tears o’erflow;
My lover ’s gone, and my good name,
Which once I valued so,
I fear must also go.
hyakunin-65.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: うらみわび ほさぬそでだに あるものを こひにくちなむ なこそをしけれ

l: In lonely solitude I dwell,
No human face I see;
And so we two must sympathize,
Oh mountain cherry tree;
I have no friend but thee.
hyakunin-66.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: もろともに あはれとおもへ やまざくら はなよりほかに しるひともなし

l: If I had made thy proffered arm
A pillow for my head
For but the moment’s time, in which
A summer’s dream had fled,
What would the world have said?
hyakunin-67.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: はるのよの ゆめばかりなる たまくらに かひなくたたむ なこそをしけれ

l: If in this troubled world of ours
I still must linger on,
My only friend shall be the moon,
Which on my sadness shone,
When other friends were gone.
hyakunin-68.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: こゝろにも あらでうきよに ながらへば こひしかるべき よはのつきかな

l: The storms, which round Mount Mimuro
Are wont to howl and scream,
Have thickly scattered maple leaves
Upon Tatsuta’s stream;
Like red brocade they seem.
hyakunin-69.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: あらしふく みむろのやまの もみぢばは たつたのかはの にしきなりけり

l: The prospect from my cottage shows
No other hut in sight;
The solitude depresses me,
Like deepening twilight
On a chill autumn night.
hyakunin-70.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: さびしさに やどをたちいでて ながむれば いづくもおなじ あきのゆふぐれ

l: This autumn night the wind blows shrill,
And would that I could catch
Its message, as it whistles through
The rushes in the thatch
And leaves of my rice-patch.
hyakunin-71.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: ゆふされば かどたのいなば おとづれて あしのまろやに あきかぜぞふく

l: The sound of ripples on the shore
Ne’er fails at Takashi;
My sleeves all worn and wet with tears
Should surely prove to thee,
I, too, will constant be.
hyakunin-72.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: おとにきく たかしのはまの あだなみは かけじやそでの ぬれもこそすれ

l: The cherry trees are blossoming
On Takasago’s height;
Oh may no mountain mist arise,
No clouds so soft and white,
To hide them from our sight.
hyakunin-73.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: たかさごの をのへのさくら さきにけり とやまのかすみ たたずもあらなむ

l: Oh! Kwannon, Patron of this hill,
The maid, for whom I pine,
Is obstinate and wayward, like
The gusts around thy shrine.
What of those prayers of mine?
hyakunin-74.src: A Hundred Verses from Old Japan
rd: うかりける ひとをはつせの やまおろし はげしかれとは いのらぬものを

l: It is a promise unfulfilled,
For which I humbly sue;

l: Two yellow orioles sing in the kingfisher-green willows;
a line of white egrets climbs the blue-green sky.
My window holds the western peaks' snow of a thousand autumns;
at my gate are moored the boats of Eastern Wu, ten thousand li from home.
Empty mountain: no one to be seen,
only the sound of voices echoing.
Light returning enters the deep wood
and shines again upon the green moss.
White stones rise out of the Jing stream;
the weather turns cold, the red leaves grow few.
There was no rain at all on the mountain path,
but the empty kingfisher-green dampens our clothes.

zh-68c845f0.t: Seeing Meng Haoran Off to Guangling at Yellow Crane Tower
l: My old friend says farewell to Yellow Crane Tower in the west;
in the third month, through mist and flowers, he goes down to Yangzhou.
The far shadow of his lone sail fades into the blue-green hills;
I see only the long river flowing to the edge of heaven.
Do you not see the waters of the Yellow River
coming down from the sky,
rushing to the sea, never to return?
Do you not see, in the bright mirrors of high halls,
people grieving over white hair:
black silk in the morning, by evening turned to snow?
When life goes your way, take your joy to the full;
never let the golden cup face the moon empty.
Heaven made my talents, so they must have a use;
spend a thousand in gold and it all comes back.
Boil the lamb, kill the ox, let us be merry;
we must drink three hundred cups at one go.
Master Cen,
Danqiu,
here comes the wine, don't put your cups down.
Let me sing you a song;
please lend me your ears.
Bells and drums, fine food and jade are not worth prizing;
I only want to stay drunk and never wake.
Since ancient times the sages have all been forgotten;
only the drinkers have left their names.
The Prince of Chen once feasted at Pingle Palace,
ten thousand a measure for wine, revelling as he pleased.
Why should the host say he is short of money?
Go straight out, buy wine, and pour for my friends.
The dappled horse,
the furs worth a thousand in gold:
call the boy, take them out and trade them for fine wine,
and with you I'll drown the sorrows of ten thousand ages.
Far up the cold mountain a stone path slants;
where the white clouds are born, there are houses.
I stop the carriage, simply for love of the maple wood at dusk:
the frosted leaves are redder than the flowers of spring.
The south of the river is lovely;
its scenery I once knew well.
At sunrise the river flowers are redder than fire;
when spring comes the river water is green as indigo.
How could I not remember the south?
Dressed in jade green, one tall tree;
ten thousand strands hang down like green silk ribbons.
Who cut out these fine leaves, I wonder?
The spring wind of the second month, like scissors.
The white sun sinks behind the mountains;
the Yellow River flows into the sea.
To see a thousand li further,
climb one more storey of the tower.
The ancients have already ridden the yellow crane away;
here only the Yellow Crane Tower is left.
Once gone, the yellow crane never returns;
for a thousand years the white clouds drift on, empty.
Across the sunlit river the trees of Hanyang stand clear;
sweet grass grows thick on Parrot Island.
Sunset: where is my home town?
Mist on the river waves makes me sad.
Red beans grow in the southern lands;
spring comes, and how many branches sprout?
I hope you will gather many:
these, more than anything, mean longing.
For a thousand li orioles sing, green against red;
water villages, mountain walls, wine flags in the wind.
Of the Southern Dynasties' four hundred and eighty temples,
how many towers and terraces stand in the misty rain?

zh-af679f9d.t: Early Spring, for Zhang the Eighteenth
l: Light rain on the capital's streets, soft as butter;
the grass's color, seen from far off, is gone up close.
This is the best moment of the year's spring,
far better than the misty willows that fill the capital.

zh-f549b18d.t: Looking at the Lu Mountain Waterfall
l: Sun on Incense Burner Peak, and purple smoke rises;
far off I see the waterfall hanging over the river.
Its flying stream plunges straight down three thousand feet:
is it the Silver River falling from the ninth heaven?
A single beam of the setting sun spreads over the water:
half the river jade-blue, half the river red.
How lovely, the night of the third of the ninth month:
dew like real pearls, the moon like a bow.

zh-7c755b22.t: Seeing Off Yuan the Second on a Mission to Anxi
l: Morning rain in Weicheng wets the light dust;
by the inn the willows are green on green, their color new.
Let me urge you to drain one more cup of wine:
west of Yang Pass you will have no old friends.
By Vermilion Bird Bridge the wild grasses flower;
at the mouth of Black Robe Lane the evening sun slants.
The swallows that once nested before the halls of the great families
now fly into the houses of ordinary people.

zh-83920f70.t: Welcome Rain on a Spring Night
l: Good rain knows its season:
it comes just as spring brings things to life.
Following the wind it slips into the night,
soaking everything, fine and soundless.
Over the country paths the clouds are all black;
only a river boat's lamp glows.
At dawn, look where it is red and wet:
the flowers hang heavy over the City of Brocade.
The nation is broken; mountains and rivers remain.
Spring in the city: grass and trees grow deep.
Moved by the times, the flowers splash tears;
grieving at parting, the birds startle the heart.
The beacon fires have burned for three months;
a letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.
I scratch my white head and the hair grows thinner,
until it can hardly hold a hairpin.

zh-55ecf9e8.t: Looking for Flowers Alone by the River (No. 5)
l: Before Master Huang's pagoda the river flows east;
spring light, lazy and drowsy, leans on a light breeze.
A cluster of peach blossom opens, belonging to no one:
lovely, the deep red shining against the pale red.
My old friend made chicken and millet
and asked me to his farm.
Green trees close round the village;
blue-green hills slant beyond the wall.
We open the window onto the threshing floor and the garden,
raise our cups and talk of mulberry and hemp.
Wait for the Double Ninth:
I'll come back for the chrysanthemums.
Blue mountains to the north of the walls,
White river winding about them;
Here we must make separation
And go out through a thousand miles of dead grass.
Mind like a floating wide cloud.
Sunset like the parting of old acquaintances
Who bow over their clasped hands at a distance.
Our horses neigh to each other
as we are departing.

l: While my hair was still cut straight across my forehead
I played about the front gate, pulling flowers.
You came by on bamboo stilts, playing horse,
You walked about my seat, playing with blue plums.
And we went on living in the village of Chokan:
Two small people, without dislike or suspicion.
At fourteen I married My Lord you.
I never laughed, being bashful.
Lowering my head, I looked at the wall.
Called to, a thousand times, I never looked back.
At fifteen I stopped scowling,
I desired my dust to be mingled with yours
Forever and forever, and forever.
Why should I climb the look out?
At sixteen you departed,
You went into far Ku-to-Yen, by the river of swirling eddies,
And you have been gone five months.
The monkeys make sorrowful noise overhead.
You dragged your feet when you went out.
By the gate now, the moss is grown, the different mosses,
Too deep to clear them away!
The leaves fall early this autumn, in wind.
The paired butterflies are already yellow with August
Over the grass in the West garden,
They hurt me,
I grow older,
If you are coming down through the narrows of the river Kiang,
Please let me know beforehand,
And I will come out to meet you,
As far as Cho-fu-Sa.

l: Blue, blue is the grass about the river
And the willows have overfilled the close garden.
And within, the mistress, in the midmost of her youth,
White, white of face, hesitates, passing the door.
Slender, she puts forth a slender hand,
And she was a courtezan in the old days,
And she has married a sot,
Who now goes drunkenly out
And leaves her too much alone.

l: Immortal Aphrodite of the broidered throne, daughter of Zeus, weaver of wiles, I pray thee break not my spirit with anguish and distress, O Queen. But come hither, if ever before thou didst hear my voice afar, and listen, and leaving thy father's golden house camest with chariot yoked, and fair fleet sparrows drew thee, flapping fast their wings around the dark earth, from heaven through mid sky. Quickly arrived they; and thou, blessed one, smiling with immortal countenance, didst ask What now is befallen me, and Why now I call, and What I in my mad heart most desire to see. 'What Beauty now wouldst thou draw to love thee? Who wrongs thee, Sappho? For even if she flies she shall soon follow, and if she rejects gifts shall yet give, and if she loves not shall soon love, however loth.' Come, I pray thee, now too, and release me from cruel cares; and all that my heart desires to accomplish, accomplish thou, and be thyself my ally.

l: The touch of Zephyr and of Spring has loosen'd Winter's thrall;
The well-dried keels are wheel'd again to sea:
The ploughman cares not for his fire, nor cattle for their stall,
And frost no more is whitening all the lea.
Now Cytherea leads the dance, the bright moon overhead;
The Graces and the Nymphs, together knit,
With rhythmic feet the meadow beat, while Vulcan, fiery red,
Heats the Cyclopian forge in Aetna's pit.
'Tis now the time to wreathe the brow with branch of myrtle green,
Or flowers, just opening to the vernal breeze;
Now Faunus claims his sacrifice among the shady treen,
Lambkin or kidling, which soe'er he please.
Pale Death, impartial, walks his round; he knocks at cottage-gate
And palace-portal. Sestius, child of bliss!
How should a mortal's hopes be long, when short his being's date?
Lo here! the fabulous ghosts, the dark abyss,
The void of the Plutonian hall, where soon as e'er you go,
No more for you shall leap the auspicious die
To seat you on the throne of wine; no more your breast shall glow
For Lycidas, the star of every eye.

horace-1.9.t: Vides ut alta stet nive candidum (Odes 1.9)
l: See, how it stands, one pile of snow,
Soracte! 'neath the pressure yield
Its groaning woods; the torrents' flow
With clear sharp ice is all congeal'd.
Heap high the logs, and melt the cold,
Good Thaliarch; draw the wine we ask,
That mellower vintage, four-year-old,
From out the cellar'd Sabine cask.
The future trust with Jove; when He
Has still'd the warring tempests' roar
On the vex'd deep, the cypress-tree
And aged ash are rock'd no more.
O, ask not what the morn will bring,
But count as gain each day that chance
May give you; sport in life's young spring,
Nor scorn sweet love, nor merry dance,
While years are green, while sullen eld
Is distant. Now the walk, the game,
The whisper'd talk at sunset held,
Each in its hour, prefer their claim.
Sweet too the laugh, whose feign'd alarm
The hiding-place of beauty tells,
The token, ravish'd from the arm
Or finger, that but ill rebels.

Thy gelid stream shall dye,
Child of the wanton herd.

Forbears to touch: sweet cool thy waters yield
To ox with ploughing tired,

'Mid honour'd founts, while I the ilex sing
Crowning the cavern, whence

ovid-pyramus.t: Pyramus and Thisbe: how the mulberry turned dark
l: As he falls on his back upon the ground, the blood spurts forth on high, not otherwise than as when a pipe is burst on the lead decaying, and shoots out afar the liquid water from the hissing flaw, and cleaves the air with its jet. The fruit of the tree, by the sprinkling of the blood, are changed to a dark tint, and the root, soaked with the gore, tints the hanging mulberries with a purple hue. Behold! not yet having banished her fear, Thisbe returns, that she may not disappoint her lover, and seeks for the youth both with her eyes and her affection, and longs to tell him how great dangers she has escaped. And when she observes the spot, and the altered appearance of the tree, she doubts if it is the same, so uncertain does the color of the fruit make her.

khayyam-211.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: O soul! lay up all earthly goods in store,
Thy mead with pleasure's flowerets spangle o'er;
And know 'tis all as dew, that decks the flowers
For one short night, and then is seen no more!
o: ایدل همه اسبابِ جهان خواسته گیر
وانگاه بران سبزه شبی چون شبنم
khayyam-243.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Vexed by this wheel of things, that pets the base.
My sorrow-laden life drags on apace;
Like rosebud, from the storm I wrap me close,
And blood-spots on my heart, like tulip, trace.
o: از گردشِ این زمانهٔ دون پرور
با صد غم و درد میبرم عمر بسر
چون غنچه بگلزارِ جهان با دلِ تنگ
چون لاله ز باغِ دهر با خونِ جگر
khayyam-245.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Though wine is banned, yet drink, for ever drink!
By day and night, with strains of music drink!
Where'er thou lightest on a cup of wine,
Spill just one drop, and take the rest, and drink!
o: با نغمه و چنگ صبح و شامش مینوش
جامی ز مئی لعل گرت دست دهد
یکقطره رها کن و تمامش مینوش
khayyam-286.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: "If heaven deny me peace and fame," I said,
"Let it be open war and shame instead;
The man who scorns bright wine had best beware,
I'll arm me with a stone, and break his head!"
o: گر صلح نیابم ز فلک جنگ اینک
ور نامِ نکو نباشدم ننگ اینک
جامِ میِ لعلِ ارغوان رنگ اینک
آنکس که نمیخورد سر و سنگ اینک
khayyam-294.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Sure of Thy grace, for sins why need I fear?
How can the pilgrim faint whilst Thou art near?
On the last day Thy grace will wash me white,
And make my "black record" to disappear.
o: با رحمتِ تو من از گنه ناندیشم
با توشهٔ تو ز رنجِ ره ناندیشم
khayyam-318.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: We make the wine-jar's lip our place of prayer,
And drink in lessons of true manhood there,
And pass our lives in taverns, if perchance
The time misspent in mosques we may repair.
o: ما جایِ نمازی بلبِ خم کردیم
خود را بمیِ لعل چو مردم کردیم
در کویِ خرابات مگر بتْوان یافت
آن عمْر که در صومعها گم کردیم
khayyam-339.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: One hand with Koran, one with wine-cup dight,
I half incline to wrong, and half to right;
The azure-marbled sky looks down on me
A sorry Moslem, yet not heathen quite.
o: گه نزدِ حلالیم و گهی نزدِ حرام
نی کافرِ مطلق نه مسلمانِ تمام
khayyam-347.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: "For once, while roses are in bloom," I said,
"I'll break the law, and please myself instead,
With blooming youths, and maidens' tulip cheeks
The plain shall blossom like a tulip-bed."
o: با سبزه خطان و لاله رخ روزی چند
بر سبزه ز جرعه لاله زاری بکنم
khayyam-358.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Though you survey, my enlightened friend,
This world of vanity from end to end,
You will discover there no other good
Than wine and rosy cheeks, you may depend!
o: در عالمِ خاک از کران تا بکران
حاصل ز جهانِ بیوفا چیزی نیست
الّا میِ لعل و عارضِ خوش پسران
khayyam-372.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Love, for ever doth heaven's wheel design
To take away thy precious life, and mine;
Sit we upon this turf, 'twill not be long
Ere turf shall grow upon my dust, and thine!
o: این چرخِ فلک بهرِ هلاکِ من و تو
قصدی دارد بجانِ پاکِ من و تو
بر سبزه نشین بتا که بس دیر نمانْد
تا سبزه برون دمد ز خاکِ من و تو
khayyam-390.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Bring forth that ruby gem of Badakhshán,
That heart's delight, that balm of Turkistán;
They say 'tis wrong for Musulmáns to drink,
But ah! where can we find a Musulmán?
o: وان راحتِ روح و راح ریحانی کو
تو می خور و غم مخور مسلمانی کو
khayyam-399.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Alas! my wasted life has gone to wrack!
What with forbidden meats, and lusts, alack!
And leaving undone what 'twas right to do,
And doing wrong, my face is very black!
o: فریاد که رفت عمر بر بیهوده
هم لقمه حرام و هم نفس آلوده
khayyam-418.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Ah! would there were a place of rest from pain,
Which we, poor pilgrims, might at last attain,
And after many thousand wintry years,
Renew our life, like flowers, and bloom again!
o: ای کاش که جایِ آرمیدن بودی
یا این ره را بسر رسیدن بودی
کاش از پیِ صد هزار سال از دلِ خاک
چون سبزه امیدِ نو دمیدن بودی
khayyam-442.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Give me a skin of wine, a crust of bread,
A pittance bare, a book of verse to read;
With thee, love, to share my lowly roof,
I would not take the Sultan's realm instead!
o: تنگی میِ لعل خواهم و دیوانی
سدِّ رمقی باید و نصفِ نانی
وانگه من و تو نشسته در ویرانی
khayyam-452.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: These ruby lips, and wine, and minstrel boys,
And lute, and harp, your dearly cherished toys,
Are mere redundancies, and you are naught.
Till you renounce the world's delusive joys.
o: تا در هوسِ لعلِ لب و جامِ مئی
تا در پیِ آوازِ دف و چنگِ نئی
اینها همه حشو است خدا میداند
تا ترکِ تعلّق نکنی هیچ نئی
khayyam-456.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Behold, where'er we turn our ravished eyes,
Sweet verdure springs, and crystal Kausars rise;
And plains, once bare as hell, now smile as heaven:
Enjoy this heaven with maids of Paradise!
o: از سبزه بهشتست وز کوثر جوئی
صحرا چه بهشت شد ز دوزخ گوئی
khayyam-459.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: When dawn doth silver the dark firmament,
Why shrills the bird of dawning his lament?
It is to show in dawn's bright looking-glass
How of thy careless life a night is spent.
o: دانی که سپیده دم خروسِ سحری
یعنی که نمودند در آئینهٔ صبْح
کز عمر شبی گذشت و تو بیخبری
khayyam-463.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: Cupbearer, come! from thy full-throated ewer
Pour blood-red wine, the world's despite to cure!
Where can I find another friend like wine,
So genuine, so solacing, so pure?
o: در ده میِ لعل لاله گونِ صافی
بکْشای ز حلقِ شیشه خونِ صافی
کامروز برون ز جامِ می نیست مرا
khayyam-464.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain

l: So long as I possess two maunds of wine,
Bread of the flower of wheat, and mutton chine,
And you, O Tulip cheeks, to share my hut,
Not every Sultan's lot can vie with mine.
o: گر دست دهد ز مغزِ گندم نانی
وز می دو منی ز گوسفندی رانی
با لاله رخی نشسته در ویرانی
عیشی بود این نه حدِّ هر سلطانی
khayyam-479.dated: c. 1100s · numbered as in Whinfield's edition; who wrote each quatrain is often uncertain
